Of the things that are quantities in themselves, some are so as substances, as the line is a quantity (for "a certain quantity" is present in the account that says what it is); others are affections and states of such a substance, as much and few, long and short, broad and narrow, deep and shallow, heavy and light, and the others of the kind. And the great and the small, and greater and smaller, said both in themselves and relative to each other, are affections of quantity in themselves; but these names are carried over to other things too. Of the things called quantities by accident, some are said so in the way it was said that the musical and the pale are quantities, by the thing they belong to being a quantity; others as motion and time are. These too are called quantities of a sort, and continuous, because the things of which they are affections are divisible. I mean not what is moved but the distance it was moved over: because that is a quantity, the motion is a quantity too, and the time because the motion is.
paragraphs.greek: ἔτι τὰ μὲν λέγεται καθʼ αὑτὰ ποσά, τὰ δὲ κατὰ συμβεβηκός, οἷον ἡ μὲν γραμμὴ ποσόν τι καθʼ ἑαυτό, τὸ δὲ μουσικὸν κατὰ συμβεβηκός. τῶν δὲ καθʼ αὑτὰ τὰ μὲν κατʼ οὐσίαν ἐστίν, οἷον ἡ γραμμὴ ποσόν τι (ἐν γὰρ τῷ λόγῳ τῷ τί ἐστι λέγοντι τὸ ποσόν τι ὑπάρχει), τὰ δὲ πάθη καὶ ἕξεις τῆς τοιαύτης ἐστὶν οὐσίας, οἷον τὸ πολὺ καὶ τὸ ὀλίγον, καὶ μακρὸν καὶ βραχύ, καὶ πλατὺ καὶ στενόν, καὶ βαθὺ καὶ ταπεινόν, καὶ βαρὺ καὶ κοῦφον, καὶ τὰ ἄλλα τὰ τοιαῦτα. ἔστι δὲ καὶ τὸ μέγα καὶ τὸ μικρὸν καὶ μεῖζον καὶ ἔλαττον, καὶ καθʼ αὑτὰ καὶ πρὸς ἄλληλα λεγόμενα, τοῦ ποσοῦ πάθη καθʼ αὑτά· μεταφέρονται μέντοι καὶ ἐπʼ ἄλλα ταῦτα τὰ ὀνόματα. τῶν δὲ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς λεγομένων ποσῶν τὰ μὲν οὕτως λέγεται ὥσπερ ἐλέχθη ὅτι τὸ μουσικὸν ποσὸν καὶ τὸ λευκὸν τῷ εἶναι ποσόν τι ᾧ ὑπάρχουσι, τὰ δὲ ὡς κίνησις καὶ χρόνος· καὶ γὰρ ταῦτα πόσʼ ἄττα λέγεται καὶ συνεχῆ τῷ ἐκεῖνα διαιρετὰ εἶναι ὧν ἐστὶ ταῦτα πάθη. λέγω δὲ οὐ τὸ κινούμενον ἀλλʼ ὃ ἐκινήθη· τῷ γὰρ ποσὸν εἶναι ἐκεῖνο καὶ ἡ κίνησις ποσή, ὁ δὲ χρόνος τῷ ταύτην.

flags.taylor: I mean not that which is moved, but the space through which it is moved
flags.why: Ross's "the space through which it is moved" is right in sense, but the Greek says only "what it was moved" (ὃ ἐκινήθη), the magnitude passed over; the same argument, that motion is continuous because the magnitude is, and time because motion is, is in Physics IV.11 (219a10-14).

notes: "The great and the small" were, for Plato as Aristotle reports him, the material principle of the Forms and the numbers, with the One as their form (Book Α, 987b20-27). Here Aristotle treats them as what they are in common speech: affections of quantity, carried over to other things by a transfer of the word.

paragraphs.modern: "Quality" is said, in one way, of the difference of the substance: man is an animal of a certain quality because he is two-footed, the horse because it is four-footed, and the circle is a figure of a certain quality because it has no angles; the difference in the substance being a quality. This, then, is one way quality is said, the difference of a substance. In another way, as of the unmoved things and the objects of mathematics: the numbers are of a certain quality, as the composite numbers that are not in one line only, but of which the plane and the solid are copies (these are the numbers that are so many times so many, or so many times so many times so many); and in general what is present in the substance besides the quantity. For the substance of each number is what it is once: of six, not what it is twice or three times, but what it is once; for six is once six.
paragraphs.greek: [τὸ] ποιὸν λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον ἡ διαφορὰ τῆς οὐσίας, οἷον ποιόν τι ἄνθρωπος ζῷον ὅτι δίπουν, ἵππος δὲ τετράπουν, καὶ κύκλος ποιόν τι σχῆμα ὅτι ἀγώνιον, ὡς τῆς διαφορᾶς τῆς κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν ποιότητος οὔσης· —ἕνα μὲν δὴ τρόπον τοῦτον λέγεται ἡ ποιότης διαφορὰ οὐσίας, ἕνα δὲ ὡς τὰ ἀκίνητα καὶ τὰ μαθηματικά, ὥσπερ οἱ ἀριθμοὶ ποιοί τινες, οἷον οἱ σύνθετοι καὶ μὴ μόνον ἐφʼ ἓν ὄντες ἀλλʼ ὧν μίμημα τὸ ἐπίπεδον καὶ τὸ στερεόν (οὗτοι δʼ εἰσὶν οἱ ποσάκις ποσοὶ ἢ ποσάκις ποσάκις ποσοί), καὶ ὅλως ὃ παρὰ τὸ ποσὸν ὑπάρχει ἐν τῇ οὐσίᾳ· οὐσία γὰρ ἑκάστου ὃ ἅπαξ, οἷον τῶν ἓξ οὐχ ὃ δὶς ἢ τρὶς εἰσὶν ἀλλʼ ὃ ἅπαξ· ἓξ γὰρ ἅπαξ ἕξ.

flags.taylor: the differentia of the essence
flags.why: Ross's "essence" here is οὐσία, "substance", which the modern version says throughout; his "differentia" is διαφορά, "difference", the word that marks off a species within its genus, as two-footed marks man off among the animals.

notes: The plane and solid numbers are the products of two and of three factors, which the Greeks drew as rectangles and boxes of units: six is a plane number, two times three, eight a solid, two times two times two. Aristotle's point is that six is not "two threes" but six, once: its substance is not its factors.

paragraphs.modern: Again, the affections of substances in motion, such as heat and cold, whiteness and blackness, heaviness and lightness, and the like, by which bodies are said to be altered when they change. Again, quality as to virtue and vice, and in general the bad and the good.
paragraphs.greek: ἔτι ὅσα πάθη τῶν κινουμένων οὐσιῶν, οἷον θερμότης καὶ ψυχρότης, καὶ λευκότης καὶ μελανία, καὶ βαρύτης καὶ κουφότης, καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα, καθʼ ἃ λέγονται καὶ ἀλλοιοῦσθαι τὰ σώματα μεταβαλλόντων. ἔτι κατʼ ἀρετὴν καὶ κακίαν καὶ ὅλως τὸ κακὸν καὶ ἀγαθόν.

paragraphs.modern: Quality, then, would be said in two ways, roughly, and of these one is the most strict. The first quality is the difference of the substance (and of this the quality in numbers is a part, for it is a difference of substances, but either of things not moved or not as moved). Next come the affections of things moved, as moved, and the differences of motions. Virtue and vice are among these affections: they show differences of the motion and of the activity by which things in motion act or are acted on well or badly. What can be moved or be active in this way is good, and what can in that way and the contrary way is bad. Good and bad signify quality most in living things, and among these most in those that have choice.
paragraphs.greek: σχεδὸν δὴ κατὰ δύο τρόπους λέγοιτʼ ἂν τὸ ποιόν, καὶ τούτων ἕνα τὸν κυριώτατον· πρώτη μὲν γὰρ ποιότης ἡ τῆς οὐσίας διαφορά (ταύτης δέ τι καὶ ἡ ἐν τοῖς ἀριθμοῖς ποιότης μέρος· διαφορὰ γάρ τις οὐσιῶν, ἀλλʼ ἢ οὐ κινουμένων ἢ οὐχ ᾗ κινούμενα), τὰ δὲ πάθη τῶν κινουμένων ᾗ κινούμενα, καὶ αἱ τῶν κινήσεων διαφοραί. ἀρετὴ δὲ καὶ κακία τῶν παθημάτων μέρος τι· διαφορὰς γὰρ δηλοῦσι τῆς κινήσεως καὶ τῆς ἐνεργείας, καθʼ ἃς ποιοῦσιν ἢ πάσχουσι καλῶς ἢ φαύλως τὰ ἐν κινήσει ὄντα· τὸ μὲν γὰρ ὡδὶ δυνάμενον κινεῖσθαι ἢ ἐνεργεῖν ἀγαθὸν τὸ δʼ ὡδὶ καὶ ἐναντίως μοχθηρόν. μάλιστα δὲ τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ τὸ κακὸν σημαίνει τὸ ποιὸν ἐπὶ τῶν ἐμψύχων, καὶ τούτων μάλιστα ἐπὶ τοῖς ἔχουσι προαίρεσιν.

flags.taylor: that which can do so in another—the contrary—way is vicious
flags.why: Ross's "vicious" renders μοχθηρόν, "bad", "wretched": the word is the general one for what is in a poor state, not only for vice of character.

paragraphs.modern: Things are called relative, some as the double to the half and the triple to the third, and in general the multiple to the submultiple and what exceeds to what is exceeded; others as what can heat to what can be heated, what can cut to what can be cut, and in general what can act to what can be acted on; others as the measurable to the measure, the knowable to knowledge and the perceptible to perception. The first are said by number, either indefinitely or definitely, to numbers themselves or to one. The double is in a definite number relative to one; the multiple is in a number relative to one, but not a definite one, not this one or that; the one-and-a-half to its reciprocal is in a definite number relative to a number; the superparticular to the subsuperparticular in an indefinite one, as the multiple to one; and what exceeds to what is exceeded is altogether indefinite in number. For number is commensurable, and number is not said of what is not commensurable; and what exceeds, relative to what is exceeded, is so much and something more, and this something is indefinite, since it may be, as it happens, either equal or not equal. All these relatives, then, are said by number and are affections of number; and so, in another way, are the equal, the like and the same. For these are all said by reference to the one: things are the same whose substance is one, like whose quality is one, equal whose quantity is one; and the one is the principle and measure of number, so that all these are called relative by number, but not in the same way.
paragraphs.greek: πρός τι λέγεται τὰ μὲν ὡς διπλάσιον πρὸς ἥμισυ καὶ τριπλάσιον πρὸς τριτημόριον, καὶ ὅλως πολλαπλάσιον πρὸς πολλοστημόριον καὶ ὑπερέχον πρὸς ὑπερεχόμενον· τὰ δʼ ὡς τὸ θερμαντικὸν πρὸς τὸ θερμαντὸν καὶ τὸ τμητικὸν πρὸς τὸ τμητόν, καὶ ὅλως τὸ ποιητικὸν πρὸς τὸ παθητικόν· τὰ δʼ ὡς τὸ μετρητὸν πρὸς τὸ μέτρον καὶ ἐπιστητὸν πρὸς ἐπιστήμην καὶ αἰσθητὸν πρὸς αἴσθησιν. λέγεται δὲ τὰ μὲν πρῶτα κατʼ ἀριθμὸν ἢ ἁπλῶς ἢ ὡρισμένως, πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἢ πρὸς ἕν (οἷον τὸ μὲν διπλάσιον πρὸς ἓν ἀριθμὸς ὡρισμένος, τὸ δὲ πολλαπλάσιον κατʼ ἀριθμὸν πρὸς ἕν, οὐχ ὡρισμένον δέ, οἷον τόνδε ἢ τόνδε· τὸ δὲ ἡμιόλιον πρὸς τὸ ὑφημιόλιον κατʼ ἀριθμὸν πρὸς ἀριθμὸν ὡρισμένον· τὸ δʼ ἐπιμόριον πρὸς τὸ ὑπεπιμόριον κατὰ ἀόριστον, ὥσπερ τὸ πολλαπλάσιον πρὸς τὸ ἕν· τὸ δʼ ὑπερέχον πρὸς τὸ ὑπερεχόμενον ὅλως ἀόριστον κατʼ ἀριθμόν· ὁ γὰρ ἀριθμὸς σύμμετρος, κατὰ μὴ συμμέτρου δὲ ἀριθμὸς οὐ λέγεται, τὸ δὲ ὑπερέχον πρὸς τὸ ὑπερεχόμενον τοσοῦτόν τέ ἐστι καὶ ἔτι, τοῦτο δʼ ἀόριστον· ὁπότερον γὰρ ἔτυχέν ἐστιν, ἢ ἴσον ἢ οὐκ ἴσον)· ταῦτά τε οὖν τὰ πρός τι πάντα κατʼ ἀριθμὸν λέγεται καὶ ἀριθμοῦ πάθη, καὶ ἔτι τὸ ἴσον καὶ ὅμοιον καὶ ταὐτὸ κατʼ ἄλλον τρόπον (κατὰ γὰρ τὸ ἓν λέγεται πάντα, ταὐτὰ μὲν γὰρ ὧν μία ἡ οὐσία, ὅμοια δʼ ὧν ἡ ποιότης μία, ἴσα δὲ ὧν τὸ ποσὸν ἕν· τὸ δʼ ἓν τοῦ ἀριθμοῦ ἀρχὴ καὶ μέτρον, ὥστε ταῦτα πάντα πρός τι λέγεται κατʼ ἀριθμὸν μέν, οὐ τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τρόπον)·

flags.taylor: but this relation may involve a ‘noncommensurate number’
flags.why: Ross's words follow another reading of the Greek: his text of 1924 says that number is not said of what is not commensurable, which the modern version follows. What exceeds may exceed by an amount that has no common measure with it, and then no number states the relation.

notes: The "superparticular" (ἐπιμόριον) is the ratio of a number to the next below it, n+1 to n, as 3:2 and 4:3, the ratios of the fifth and the fourth in music; the one-and-a-half (ἡμιόλιον) is 3:2 itself. Plato builds the soul of the world from such ratios in the Timaeus (35b-36b).

paragraphs.modern: What can act and what can be acted on are relative by a power to act and a power to be acted on, and by the activities of the powers: what can heat is relative to what can be heated because it can heat it, and again what heats to what is heated, and what cuts to what is cut, as being active. Relatives by number have no activities, except in the way stated elsewhere; activities in the sense of motion they do not have. Of relatives by power, some are relative by times as well: what has made to what has been made, and what will make to what will be made. It is in this way that a father is called the father of a son: the one has acted, the other has been acted on. Again, some are relative by privation of power, as the incapable and things said so, such as the invisible.
paragraphs.greek: τὰ δὲ ποιητικὰ καὶ παθητικὰ κατὰ δύναμιν ποιητικὴν καὶ παθητικὴν καὶ ἐνεργείας τὰς τῶν δυνάμεων, οἷον τὸ θερμαντικὸν πρὸς τὸ θερμαντὸν ὅτι δύναται, καὶ πάλιν τὸ θερμαῖνον πρὸς τὸ θερμαινόμενον καὶ τὸ τέμνον πρὸς τὸ τεμνόμενον ὡς ἐνεργοῦντα. τῶν δὲ κατʼ ἀριθμὸν οὐκ εἰσὶν ἐνέργειαι ἀλλʼ ἢ ὃν τρόπον ἐν ἑτέροις εἴρηται· αἱ δὲ κατὰ κίνησιν ἐνέργειαι οὐχ ὑπάρχουσιν. τῶν δὲ κατὰ δύναμιν καὶ κατὰ χρόνους ἤδη λέγονται πρός τι οἷον τὸ πεποιηκὸς πρὸς τὸ πεποιημένον καὶ τὸ ποιῆσον πρὸς τὸ ποιησόμενον. οὕτω γὰρ καὶ πατὴρ υἱοῦ λέγεται πατήρ· τὸ μὲν γὰρ πεποιηκὸς τὸ δὲ πεπονθός τί ἐστιν. ἔτι ἔνια κατὰ στέρησιν δυνάμεως, ὥσπερ τὸ ἀδύνατον καὶ ὅσα οὕτω λέγεται, οἷον τὸ ἀόρατον.

paragraphs.modern: Things called relative by number and by power, then, are all relative because just what they are is said to be of something else, not because something else is relative to them. But the measurable, the knowable and the thinkable are called relative because something else is said with reference to them. For the thinkable signifies that there is thought of it; but thought is not relative to that of which it is the thought (for the same thing would have been said twice). Likewise sight is sight of something, not of that of which it is the sight (though it is true to say so), but relative to colour or something else of the kind; said the other way, the same thing will be said twice: that sight is of that of which it is the sight.
paragraphs.greek: τὰ μὲν οὖν κατʼ ἀριθμὸν καὶ δύναμιν λεγόμενα πρός τι πάντα ἐστὶ πρός τι τῷ ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἄλλου λέγεσθαι αὐτὸ ὅ ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ μὴ τῷ ἄλλο πρὸς ἐκεῖνο· τὸ δὲ μετρητὸν καὶ τὸ ἐπιστητὸν καὶ τὸ διανοητὸν τῷ ἄλλο πρὸς αὐτὸ λέγεσθαι πρός τι λέγονται. τό τε γὰρ διανοητὸν σημαίνει ὅτι ἔστιν αὐτοῦ διάνοια, οὐκ ἔστι δʼ ἡ διάνοια πρὸς τοῦτο οὗ ἐστὶ διάνοια (δὶς γὰρ ταὐτὸν εἰρημένον ἂν εἴη), ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τινός ἐστιν ἡ ὄψις ὄψις, οὐχ οὗ ἐστὶν ὄψις (καίτοι γʼ ἀληθὲς τοῦτο εἰπεῖν) ἀλλὰ πρὸς χρῶμα ἢ πρὸς ἄλλο τι τοιοῦτον. ἐκείνως δὲ δὶς τὸ αὐτὸ λεχθήσεται, ὅτι ἐστὶν οὗ ἐστὶν ἡ ὄψις.
notes: Plato's Charmides (167c-169a) asks whether there can be a knowledge whose object is only knowledge, as sight would see only sight; and the Republic (438b-e) sets out the rule that a relative is of its own correlative, knowledge of the knowable. Aristotle's third kind of relative, the knowable and the measurable, is the one that the Platonists set highest: the intelligible is prior to the intellect that knows it.

paragraphs.modern: Things said to be relative in themselves are said so in these ways; others because their genera are such: medicine is a relative because its genus, knowledge, seems to be a relative. Again, the properties by which the things having them are called relative: equality because the equal is relative, and likeness because the like is. Others are relative by accident: a man is relative because it happens to him to be double, and the double is a relative; or the white, if it happens to the same thing to be double and white.
paragraphs.greek: τὰ μὲν οὖν καθʼ ἑαυτὰ λεγόμενα πρός τι τὰ μὲν οὕτω λέγεται, τὰ δὲ ἂν τὰ γένη αὐτῶν ᾖ τοιαῦτα, οἷον ἡ ἰατρικὴ τῶν πρός τι ὅτι τὸ γένος αὐτῆς ἡ ἐπιστήμη δοκεῖ εἶναι πρός τι· ἔτι καθʼ ὅσα τὰ ἔχοντα λέγεται πρός τι, οἷον ἰσότης ὅτι τὸ ἴσον καὶ ὁμοιότης ὅτι τὸ ὅμοιον· τὰ δὲ κατὰ συμβεβηκός, οἷον ἅνθρωπος πρός τι ὅτι συμβέβηκεν αὐτῷ διπλασίῳ εἶναι, τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶ τῶν πρός τι· ἢ τὸ λευκόν, εἰ τῷ αὐτῷ συμβέβηκε διπλασίῳ καὶ λευκῷ εἶναι.

paragraphs.modern: "Complete" is said, in one way, of that outside which not even one of its parts can be found: the complete time of each thing is the time outside which no time can be found that is a part of it. And of what, in excellence and in doing well, has nothing beyond it in its kind: as a doctor is complete and a flute-player complete, when they lack nothing in the form of their proper virtue. (So too, by a transfer of the word, we speak of bad things, and say a complete informer and a complete thief, since we even call them good, a good thief and a good informer. And virtue is a kind of completion: for each thing is complete, and every substance complete, when in the form of its proper virtue it lacks no part of its natural magnitude.)
paragraphs.greek: τέλειον λέγεται ἓν μὲν οὗ μὴ ἔστιν ἔξω τι λαβεῖν μηδὲ ἓν μόριον (οἷον χρόνος τέλειος ἑκάστου οὗτος οὗ μὴ ἔστιν ἔξω λαβεῖν χρόνον τινὰ ὃς τούτου μέρος ἐστὶ τοῦ χρόνου), καὶ τὸ κατʼ ἀρετὴν καὶ τὸ εὖ μὴ ἔχον ὑπερβολὴν πρὸς τὸ γένος, οἷον τέλειος ἰατρὸς καὶ τέλειος αὐλητὴς ὅταν κατὰ τὸ εἶδος τῆς οἰκείας ἀρετῆς μηθὲν ἐλλείπωσιν (οὕτω δὲ μεταφέροντες καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κακῶν λέγομεν συκοφάντην τέλειον καὶ κλέπτην τέλειον, ἐπειδὴ καὶ ἀγαθοὺς λέγομεν αὐτούς, οἷον κλέπτην ἀγαθὸν καὶ συκοφάντην ἀγαθόν· καὶ ἡ ἀρετὴ τελείωσίς τις· ἕκαστον γὰρ τότε τέλειον καὶ οὐσία πᾶσα τότε τελεία, ὅταν κατὰ τὸ εἶδος τῆς οἰκείας ἀρετῆς μηδὲν ἐλλείπῃ μόριον τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν μεγέθους)·

flags.taylor: and speak of a complete scandal-monger and a complete thief
flags.why: Ross's "scandal-monger" renders συκοφάντης, the "informer" of Athens, who brought prosecutions for gain or to blackmail; the word is the root of "sycophant", which has since come to mean a flatterer.

flags.taylor: The perfect is denominated that of which no part can be
flags.why: Taylor's "perfect" and Ross's "complete" both render τέλειον, which is from τέλος, "end": what has reached its end, lacks nothing. The modern version says "complete", and keeps the link with "end" in the third sense.

paragraphs.modern: Again, things that have reached their end, if it is good, are called complete; for things are complete by having their end. So, since the end is something last, we carry the word over to bad things too, and say that a thing has been completely ruined and completely destroyed, when nothing is lacking to its destruction and its badness, but it is at the last point. That is why death too is called the end by a transfer of the word, because both are last things; but that for the sake of which, the final end, is an end too. Things called complete in themselves, then, are called so in all these ways: some because, in doing well, they lack nothing and have nothing beyond them, and nothing of theirs can be found outside; others because, in general, they have nothing beyond them in each kind and nothing of theirs is outside. The others are now called complete by reference to these, because they make something of the kind, or have it, or fit it, or are in one way or another related to the things first called complete.
paragraphs.greek: ἔτι οἷς ὑπάρχει τὸ τέλος, σπουδαῖον ὄν, ταῦτα λέγεται τέλεια· κατὰ γὰρ τὸ ἔχειν τὸ τέλος τέλεια, ὥστʼ ἐπεὶ τὸ τέλος τῶν ἐσχάτων τί ἐστι, καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ φαῦλα μεταφέροντες λέγομεν τελείως ἀπολωλέναι καὶ τελείως ἐφθάρθαι, ὅταν μηδὲν ἐλλείπῃ τῆς φθορᾶς καὶ τοῦ κακοῦ ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ τῷ ἐσχάτῳ ᾖ· διὸ καὶ ἡ τελευτὴ κατὰ μεταφορὰν λέγεται τέλος, ὅτι ἄμφω ἔσχατα· τέλος δὲ καὶ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα ἔσχατον. τὰ μὲν οὖν καθʼ αὑτὰ λεγόμενα τέλεια τοσαυταχῶς λέγεται, τὰ μὲν τῷ κατὰ τὸ εὖ μηδὲν ἐλλείπειν μηδʼ ἔχειν ὑπερβολὴν μηδὲ ἔξω τι λαβεῖν, τὰ δʼ ὅλως κατὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν ὑπερβολὴν ἐν ἑκάστῳ γένει μηδʼ εἶναί τι ἔξω· τὰ δὲ ἄλλα ἤδη κατὰ ταῦτα τῷ ἢ ποιεῖν τι τοιοῦτον ἢ ἔχειν ἢ ἁρμόττειν τούτῳ ἢ ἁμῶς γέ πως λέγεσθαι πρὸς τὰ πρώτως λεγόμενα τέλεια.
notes: For the Platonists the complete is the mark of the first causes: what is complete gives of itself to what comes after it, as Proclus says (Elements of Theology 25), and the most complete is the cause of the most things. Plato's maker of the world makes it complete, a whole of wholes, lacking nothing (Timaeus 32c-34b).

paragraphs.modern: "Limit" is said of the last point of each thing, the first point outside which nothing of it can be found and the first within which all of it is; and of whatever is the form of a magnitude or of what has magnitude; and of the end of each thing (such is that to which the motion and the action go, and not that from which they go, though sometimes it is both, that from which and that to which, and that for the sake of which); and of the substance of each thing, what it is to be for each. For this is the limit of knowledge; and if of knowledge, of the thing too. So it is plain that limit is said in as many ways as principle, and in more: for the principle is a limit, but not every limit is a principle.
paragraphs.greek: πέρας λέγεται τό τε ἔσχατον ἑκάστου καὶ οὗ ἔξω μηδὲν ἔστι λαβεῖν πρώτου καὶ οὗ ἔσω πάντα πρώτου, καὶ ὃ ἂν ᾖ εἶδος μεγέθους ἢ ἔχοντος μέγεθος, καὶ τὸ τέλος ἑκάστου (τοιοῦτον δʼ ἐφʼ ὃ ἡ κίνησις καὶ ἡ πρᾶξις, καὶ οὐκ ἀφʼ οὗ—ὁτὲ δὲ ἄμφω, καὶ ἀφʼ οὗ καὶ ἐφʼ ὃ καὶ τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα), καὶ ἡ οὐσία ἡ ἑκάστου καὶ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι ἑκάστῳ· τῆς γνώσεως γὰρ τοῦτο πέρας· εἰ δὲ τῆς γνώσεως, καὶ τοῦ πράγματος. ὥστε φανερὸν ὅτι ὁσαχῶς τε ἡ ἀρχὴ λέγεται, τοσαυταχῶς καὶ τὸ πέρας, καὶ ἔτι πλεοναχῶς· ἡ μὲν γὰρ ἀρχὴ πέρας τι, τὸ δὲ πέρας οὐ πᾶν ἀρχή.
notes: "Limit" (πέρας) is a word of the Philebus (23c-27c), where everything that is is a mixture of limit and the unlimited, and of the Pythagoreans before Plato. The Platonists after Plotinus made limit and the unlimited the first pair after the One (Proclus, Elements of Theology 89-92, and Platonic Theology III).

paragraphs.modern: "That in virtue of which" is said in many ways. In one way it is the form and the substance of each thing, as that in virtue of which one is good is the good itself; in another, the first thing in which something naturally comes to be, as colour in the surface. That in virtue of which, then, said in the first way, is the form; in the second way, the matter of each thing and the first underlying thing of each. In general "that in virtue of which" will be said in as many ways as "cause": we say "in virtue of what has he come?" or "for the sake of what has he come?", and "in virtue of what has he reasoned falsely, or reasoned?", or "what is the cause of the reasoning, or of the false reasoning?" Again, "that in virtue of which" is said of position: "that by which he stands" or "that along which he walks"; for all these signify place and position.
paragraphs.greek: τὸ καθʼ ὃ λέγεται πολλαχῶς, ἕνα μὲν τρόπον τὸ εἶδος καὶ ἡ οὐσία ἑκάστου πράγματος, οἷον καθʼ ὃ ἀγαθός, αὐτὸ ἀγαθόν, ἕνα δὲ ἐν ᾧ πρώτῳ πέφυκε γίγνεσθαι, οἷον τὸ χρῶμα ἐν τῇ ἐπιφανείᾳ. τὸ μὲν οὖν πρώτως λεγόμενον καθʼ ὃ τὸ εἶδός ἐστι, δευτέρως δὲ ὡς ἡ ὕλη ἑκάστου καὶ τὸ ὑποκείμενον ἑκάστῳ πρῶτον. ὅλως δὲ τὸ καθʼ ὃ ἰσαχῶς καὶ τὸ αἴτιον ὑπάρξει· κατὰ τί γὰρ ἐλήλυθεν ἢ οὗ ἕνεκα ἐλήλυθε λέγεται, καὶ κατὰ τί παραλελόγισται ἢ συλλελόγισται, ἢ τί τὸ αἴτιον τοῦ συλλογισμοῦ ἢ παραλογισμοῦ. ἔτι δὲ τὸ καθʼ ὃ τὸ κατὰ θέσιν λέγεται, καθʼ ὃ ἕστηκεν ἢ καθʼ ὃ βαδίζει· πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα τόπον σημαίνει καὶ θέσιν.

flags.taylor: that in virtue of which a man is good is the good itself
flags.why: Ross's words follow his own correction of the Greek (his note says so), which the 1924 text keeps: "the good itself" (αὐτὸ ἀγαθόν). The Platonists heard in it the Form of the Good, by which good things are good (Republic 505a, 508e); Aristotle means the goodness in the man, his form.

notes: Ross's note says that "no English word or phrase has quite the same ambiguity" as the Greek καθ' ὅ, which can mean "in virtue of which", "according to which" and, of place, "by which" or "along which".

paragraphs.modern: So "in itself" too must be said in many ways. In one way, what it is to be for each thing: Callias is in himself Callias, and what it is to be Callias. In another, whatever is present in the what-it-is: Callias is in himself an animal, for animal is present in his account, since Callias is a certain animal. Again, if a thing has received something first in itself or in one of its parts: the surface is white in itself, and a man lives in himself, for the soul, in which life first is, is a part of the man. Again, what has no other cause: man has many causes, animal, two-footed, but still man is man in himself. Again, whatever belongs to a thing alone, and as alone; and so what is separated is in itself.
paragraphs.greek: ὥστε καὶ τὸ καθʼ αὑτὸ πολλαχῶς ἀνάγκη λέγεσθαι. ἓν μὲν γὰρ καθʼ αὑτὸ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι ἑκάστῳ, οἷον ὁ Καλλίας καθʼ αὑτὸν Καλλίας καὶ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι Καλλίᾳ· ἓν δὲ ὅσα ἐν τῷ τί ἐστιν ὑπάρχει, οἷον ζῷον ὁ Καλλίας καθʼ αὑτόν· ἐν γὰρ τῷ λόγῳ ἐνυπάρχει τὸ ζῷον· ζῷον γάρ τι ὁ Καλλίας. ἔτι δὲ εἰ ἐν αὑτῷ δέδεκται πρώτῳ ἢ τῶν αὑτοῦ τινί, οἷον ἡ ἐπιφάνεια λευκὴ καθʼ ἑαυτήν, καὶ ζῇ ὁ ἄνθρωπος καθʼ αὑτόν· ἡ γὰρ ψυχὴ μέρος τι τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, ἐν ᾗ πρώτῃ τὸ ζῆν. ἔτι οὗ μὴ ἔστιν ἄλλο αἴτιον· τοῦ γὰρ ἀνθρώπου πολλὰ αἴτια, τὸ ζῷον, τὸ δίπουν, ἀλλʼ ὅμως καθʼ αὑτὸν ἄνθρωπος ὁ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν. ἔτι ὅσα μόνῳ ὑπάρχει καὶ ᾗ μόνον διʼ αὐτὸ κεχωρισμένον καθʼ αὑτό.

flags.taylor: the essence of each thing, e.g. Callias is in virtue of himself Callias and the essence of Callias
flags.why: Ross's "essence" is τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι, "what it is to be", as everywhere in this work. "In itself" (καθ' αὑτό) is the Latin "per se"; the senses here are those of Posterior Analytics I.4 (73a34-b24).

paragraphs.modern: "Disposition" is said of the order of what has parts, either in place, or in power, or in form. For there must be some position, as the word "disposition" itself shows.
paragraphs.greek: διάθεσις λέγεται τοῦ ἔχοντος μέρη τάξις ἢ κατὰ τόπον ἢ κατὰ δύναμιν ἢ κατʼ εἶδος· θέσιν γὰρ δεῖ τινὰ εἶναι, ὥσπερ καὶ τοὔνομα δηλοῖ ἡ διάθεσις.

flags.taylor: either according^ to place, or according to capacity
flags.why: Taylor's "capacity" renders δύναμις, "power", which the modern version says here; and the word "disposition" (διάθεσις, "placing apart") contains θέσις, "position", as the Latin "dispositio" contains "positio".

paragraphs.modern: "Having" (ἕξις) is said, in one way, of a kind of activity of the haver and the had, as a kind of action or motion: when one thing makes and another is made, there is a making between them; so between the one who has a garment and the garment had there is a having. It is plain, then, that one cannot have this having: it would go on without end, if one could have the having of what is had. In another way, ἕξις is said of a disposition by which what is disposed is disposed well or badly, either in itself or relative to something else: health is a state, for it is such a disposition. Again, a part of such a disposition is called a state; and so the virtue of the parts is a state.
paragraphs.greek: ἕξις δὲ λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον οἷον ἐνέργειά τις τοῦ ἔχοντος καὶ ἐχομένου, ὥσπερ πρᾶξίς τις ἢ κίνησις (ὅταν γὰρ τὸ μὲν ποιῇ τὸ δὲ ποιῆται, ἔστι ποίησις μεταξύ· οὕτω καὶ τοῦ ἔχοντος ἐσθῆτα καὶ τῆς ἐχομένης ἐσθῆτος ἔστι μεταξὺ ἕξις)·—ταύτην μὲν οὖν φανερὸν ὅτι οὐκ ἐνδέχεται ἔχειν ἕξιν (εἰς ἄπειρον γὰρ βαδιεῖται, εἰ τοῦ ἐχομένου ἔσται ἔχειν τὴν ἕξιν), ἄλλον δὲ τρόπον ἕξις λέγεται διάθεσις καθʼ ἣν ἢ εὖ ἢ κακῶς διάκειται τὸ διακείμενον, καὶ ἢ καθʼ αὑτὸ ἢ πρὸς ἄλλο, οἷον ἡ ὑγίεια ἕξις τις· διάθεσις γάρ ἐστι τοιαύτη. ἔτι ἕξις λέγεται ἂν ᾖ μόριον διαθέσεως τοιαύτης· διὸ καὶ ἡ τῶν μερῶν ἀρετὴ ἕξις τίς ἐστιν.

flags.taylor: means (1) a kind of activity of the haver and the had
flags.why: Ross's "activity" is ἐνέργεια, "actuality", "being at work", here the having as it is going on. The one Greek word ἕξις does duty, as Ross's note says, for "having", "habit" and "state": the modern version says "having" in the first sense and "state" in the others. Virtue, the Ethics says (II.5), is a state in this second sense.

paragraphs.modern: "Affection" is said, in one way, of a quality by which a thing can be altered, as white and black, sweet and bitter, heaviness and lightness, and all the others of the kind. In another, of the activities of these, the alterations already taking place. Again, more than these, of the harmful alterations and motions, and above all of painful harms. Again, great misfortunes and pains are called affections.
paragraphs.greek: πάθος λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον ποιότης καθʼ ἣν ἀλλοιοῦσθαι ἐνδέχεται, οἷον τὸ λευκὸν καὶ τὸ μέλαν, καὶ γλυκὺ καὶ πικρόν, καὶ βαρύτης καὶ κουφότης, καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα τοιαῦτα· ἕνα δὲ αἱ τούτων ἐνέργειαι καὶ ἀλλοιώσεις ἤδη. ἔτι τούτων μᾶλλον αἱ βλαβεραὶ ἀλλοιώσεις καὶ κινήσεις, καὶ μάλιστα αἱ λυπηραὶ βλάβαι. ἔτι τὰ μεγέθη τῶν συμφορῶν καὶ λυπηρῶν πάθη λέγεται.

flags.taylor: Passion is called in the first place quality
flags.why: Taylor's "passion" renders πάθος, from πάσχειν, "to undergo", "to be acted on": what happens to a thing, not only a strong feeling. The modern version says "affection", Ross's word; the last senses, harms and misfortunes, are where the English "suffering" and "passion" come from.

paragraphs.modern: "Privation" is said, in one way, if a thing does not have one of the attributes that things naturally have, even if it would not itself naturally have it: so a plant is said to be deprived of eyes. In another way, if it does not have what it, or its genus, would naturally have: so a blind man and a mole are deprived of sight in different ways, the one in respect of its genus, the other in respect of himself. Again, if it does not have it although it would naturally have it, and when it would naturally have it: blindness is a privation, but one is not blind at any age, only if one does not have sight at the age at which one would naturally have it. Likewise if it does not have it in the medium in which, by the organ by which, relative to the thing to which, and in the manner in which it would naturally have it. Again, the violent taking away of anything is called privation.
paragraphs.greek: στέρησις λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον ἂν μὴ ἔχῃ τι τῶν πεφυκότων ἔχεσθαι, κἂν μὴ αὐτὸ ᾖ πεφυκὸς ἔχειν, οἷον φυτὸν ὀμμάτων ἐστερῆσθαι λέγεται· ἕνα δὲ ἂν πεφυκὸς ἔχειν, ἢ αὐτὸ ἢ τὸ γένος, μὴ ἔχῃ, οἷον ἄλλως ἄνθρωπος ὁ τυφλὸς ὄψεως ἐστέρηται καὶ ἀσπάλαξ, τὸ μὲν κατὰ τὸ γένος τὸ δὲ καθʼ αὑτό. ἔτι ἂν πεφυκὸς καὶ ὅτε πέφυκεν ἔχειν μὴ ἔχῃ· ἡ γὰρ τυφλότης στέρησίς τις, τυφλὸς δʼ οὐ κατὰ πᾶσαν ἡλικίαν, ἀλλʼ ἐν ᾗ πέφυκεν ἔχειν, ἂν μὴ ἔχῃ. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἐν ᾧ ἂν ᾖ πεφυκὸς καὶ καθʼ ὃ καὶ πρὸς ὃ καὶ ὥς, ἂν μὴ ἔχῃ [πεφυκός]. ἔτι ἡ βιαία ἑκάστου ἀφαίρεσις στέρησις λέγεται.
notes: The mole, Aristotle says in On the Soul (III.1, 425a10-11) and the History of Animals (I.9, 491b28-34; IV.8, 533a3-12), has eyes beneath the skin, but cannot see: it lacks sight in respect of its genus, the animals, which naturally see.

paragraphs.modern: Privations are said in as many ways as negations from the alpha (our "un-" or "in-"). A thing is called unequal by not having the equality it would naturally have; invisible either by having no colour at all or by having it poorly; footless either by having no feet at all or by having poor ones. Again, by having little of it, as the stoneless (of fruit): this is having it poorly in a way. Again, by not having it easily or not well: the uncuttable is not only what cannot be cut but what cannot be cut easily or well. Again, by not having it at all: it is not the one-eyed man who is called blind, but the one who has no sight in either eye. That is why not everyone is good or bad, just or unjust: there is also the middle.
paragraphs.greek: καὶ ὁσαχῶς δὲ αἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ α ἀποφάσεις λέγονται, τοσαυταχῶς καὶ αἱ στερήσεις λέγονται· ἄνισον μὲν γὰρ τῷ μὴ ἔχειν ἰσότητα πεφυκὸς λέγεται, ἀόρατον δὲ καὶ τῷ ὅλως μὴ ἔχειν χρῶμα καὶ τῷ φαύλως, καὶ ἄπουν καὶ τῷ μὴ ἔχειν ὅλως πόδας καὶ τῷ φαύλους. ἔτι καὶ τῷ μικρὸν ἔχειν, οἷον τὸ ἀπύρηνον· τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶ τὸ φαύλως πως ἔχειν. ἔτι τῷ μὴ ῥᾳδίως ἢ τῷ μὴ καλῶς, οἷον τὸ ἄτμητον οὐ μόνον τῷ μὴ τέμνεσθαι ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ μὴ ῥᾳδίως ἢ μὴ καλῶς. ἔτι τῷ πάντῃ μὴ ἔχειν· τυφλὸς γὰρ οὐ λέγεται ὁ ἑτερόφθαλμος ἀλλʼ ὁ ἐν ἀμφοῖν μὴ ἔχων ὄψιν· διὸ οὐ πᾶς ἀγαθὸς ἢ κακός, ἢ δίκαιος ἢ ἄδικος, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ μεταξύ.

flags.taylor: Again, a privative term may be used because the thing has little of the
flags.why: Ross's page has lost a line here (at 1022b and 1023a): his "kernelless" is ἀπύρηνον, "stoneless", said of a fruit with a small stone, and the lost words say that this is having it poorly. Ross's page has lost the end of the paragraph too, from "one-eyed" to "That is why" (at 1023a); the modern version follows the Greek in both places.

paragraphs.modern: "To have" is said in many ways. In one way, to treat a thing according to one's own nature or one's own impulse: so a fever is said to have a man, and tyrants their cities, and those who wear clothes their clothes. In another way, that in which something is present, as in what can receive it, is said to have it: the bronze has the form of the statue, and the body the disease. In another way, as the container holds what is contained: what is in a container is said to be held by it, as we say that the vessel holds the liquid, the city men and the ship sailors; and so the whole holds the parts. Again, what prevents a thing from moving or acting by its own impulse is said to hold it: as pillars hold the weights placed on them, and as the poets make Atlas hold up the heaven, which would otherwise fall onto the earth, as some of the natural philosophers also say. In this way too what holds things together is said to hold the things it holds together, since they would otherwise separate, each by its own impulse. And "being in something" is said in like ways, following "having".
paragraphs.greek: τὸ ἔχειν λέγεται πολλαχῶς, ἕνα μὲν τρόπον τὸ ἄγειν κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ φύσιν ἢ κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ ὁρμήν, διὸ λέγεται πυρετός τε ἔχειν τὸν ἄνθρωπον καὶ οἱ τύραννοι τὰς πόλεις καὶ τὴν ἐσθῆτα οἱ ἀμπεχόμενοι· ἕνα δʼ ἐν ᾧ ἄν τι ὑπάρχῃ ὡς δεκτικῷ, οἷον ὁ χαλκὸς ἔχει τὸ εἶδος τοῦ ἀνδριάντος καὶ τὴν νόσον τὸ σῶμα· ἕνα δὲ ὡς τὸ περιέχον τὰ περιεχόμενα· ἐν ᾧ γάρ ἐστι περιέχοντι, ἔχεσθαι ὑπὸ τούτου λέγεται, οἷον τὸ ἀγγεῖον ἔχειν τὸ ὑγρόν φαμεν καὶ τὴν πόλιν ἀνθρώπους καὶ τὴν ναῦν ναύτας, οὕτω δὲ καὶ τὸ ὅλον ἔχειν τὰ μέρη. ἔτι τὸ κωλῦον κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ ὁρμήν τι κινεῖσθαι ἢ πράττειν ἔχειν λέγεται τοῦτο αὐτό, οἷον καὶ οἱ κίονες τὰ ἐπικείμενα βάρη, καὶ ὡς οἱ ποιηταὶ τὸν Ἄτλαντα ποιοῦσι τὸν οὐρανὸν ἔχειν ὡς συμπεσόντʼ ἂν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, ὥσπερ καὶ τῶν φυσιολόγων τινές φασιν· τοῦτον δὲ τὸν τρόπον καὶ τὸ συνέχον λέγεται ἃ συνέχει ἔχειν, ὡς διαχωρισθέντα ἂν κατὰ τὴν αὑτοῦ ὁρμὴν ἕκαστον. καὶ τὸ ἔν τινι δὲ εἶναι ὁμοτρόπως λέγεται καὶ ἑπομένως τῷ ἔχειν.

flags.taylor: as pillars hold the incumbent
flags.why: Ross's page has lost words here (at 1023a), those on Atlas holding up the heaven; the modern version follows the Greek. "Some of the natural philosophers": On the Heavens (II.1, 284a18-26) says that some thought the heaven needs a support; Aristotle's own heaven moves by its nature and needs none.

notes: Ross's page has lost words in the first and third senses as well (at 1023a), from "according to one's own impulse" to "tyrants", and from "what is in a container" to "the vessel"; the modern version follows the Greek.

paragraphs.modern: "To be from something" is said, in one way, of that from which a thing is, as from matter; and this in two ways, either according to the first genus or according to the last species: in one way all things that can be melted are from water, in another the statue is from bronze. In another way, as from the first principle that moved it: "from what came the fight? From abuse", because this was the principle of the fight. In another way, from the compound of matter and shape, as the parts are from the whole, the verse from the Iliad and the stones from the house: for the shape is the end, and what has its end is complete. In another way, as the form is from its part: man from two-footed, and the syllable from the letter; for this is another way than the way the statue is from bronze, since the composite substance is from sensible matter, but the form too is from the matter of the form.
paragraphs.greek: τὸ ἔκ τινος εἶναι λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον ἐξ οὗ ἐστὶν ὡς ὕλης, καὶ τοῦτο διχῶς, ἢ κατὰ τὸ πρῶτον γένος ἢ κατὰ τὸ ὕστατον εἶδος, οἷον ἔστι μὲν ὡς ἅπαντα τὰ τηκτὰ ἐξ ὕδατος, ἔστι δʼ ὡς ἐκ χαλκοῦ ὁ ἀνδριάς· ἕνα δʼ ὡς ἐκ τῆς πρώτης κινησάσης ἀρχῆς (οἷον ἐκ τίνος ἡ μάχη; ἐκ λοιδορίας, ὅτι αὕτη ἀρχὴ τῆς μάχης)· ἕνα δʼ ἐκ τοῦ συνθέτου ἐκ τῆς ὕλης καὶ τῆς μορφῆς, ὥσπερ ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου τὰ μέρη καὶ ἐκ τῆς Ἰλιάδος τὸ ἔπος καὶ ἐκ τῆς οἰκίας οἱ λίθοι· τέλος μὲν γάρ ἐστιν ἡ μορφή, τέλειον δὲ τὸ ἔχον τέλος. τὰ δὲ ὡς ἐκ τοῦ μέρους τὸ εἶδος, οἷον ἅνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ δίποδος καὶ ἡ συλλαβὴ ἐκ τοῦ στοιχείου· ἄλλως γὰρ τοῦτο καὶ ὁ ἀνδριὰς ἐκ χαλκοῦ· ἐκ τῆς αἰσθητῆς γὰρ ὕλης ἡ συνθετὴ οὐσία, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ εἶδος ἐκ τῆς τοῦ εἴδους ὕλης.
notes: "The matter of the form": the parts of a definition, genus and difference, of which the form is composed as a statue of its bronze. Book Ζ (chapters 10 to 12) and Book Η (chapter 6) take this "intelligible matter" further.

paragraphs.modern: Some things, then, are said to be from something in these ways; others if one of these ways belongs to a part of it: as the child is from father and mother, and plants from the earth, because they are from some part of these. In another way, what comes after something in time: as night is from day, and storm from fair weather, because the one comes after the other. Of these, some are said so because they change into each other, as with the ones just named; others only because they follow one another in time, as "the voyage was from the equinox", because it took place after the equinox, and "the Thargelia are from the Dionysia", because they come after the Dionysia.
paragraphs.greek: τὰ μὲν οὖν οὕτω λέγεται, τὰ δʼ ἐὰν κατὰ μέρος τι τούτων τις ὑπάρχῃ τῶν τρόπων, οἷον ἐκ πατρὸς καὶ μητρὸς τὸ τέκνον καὶ ἐκ γῆς τὰ φυτά, ὅτι ἔκ τινος μέρους αὐτῶν. ἕνα δὲ μεθʼ ὃ τῷ χρόνῳ, οἷον ἐξ ἡμέρας νὺξ καὶ ἐξ εὐδίας χειμών, ὅτι τοῦτο μετὰ τοῦτο· τούτων δὲ τὰ μὲν τῷ ἔχειν μεταβολὴν εἰς ἄλληλα οὕτω λέγεται, ὥσπερ καὶ τὰ νῦν εἰρημένα, τὰ δὲ τῷ κατὰ τὸν χρόνον ἐφεξῆς μόνον, οἷον ἐξ ἰσημερίας ἐγένετο ὁ πλοῦς ὅτι μετʼ ἰσημερίαν ἐγένετο, καὶ ἐκ Διονυσίων Θαργήλια ὅτι μετὰ τὰ Διονύσια.

flags.taylor: the child comes from its father and mother and plants come from
flags.why: Ross's page has lost the rest of the chapter (at 1023b), on what comes after in time; the modern version follows the Greek. The Dionysia, the great festival of Dionysus, came in spring; the Thargelia, the festival of Apollo, two months after.

paragraphs.modern: "Part" is said, in one way, of that into which a quantity may be divided in any way: for what is taken away from a quantity, as a quantity, is always called a part of it, as two is called in a way a part of three. In another way, only of those that measure such a quantity exactly; so that two is in one way said to be a part of three, and in another not. Again, the things into which the kind might be divided, apart from quantity, are called its parts too: so people say the species are parts of the genus. Again, the things into which a whole is divided or of which it is composed, whether the whole is the form or what has the form: of the bronze sphere or the bronze cube, both the bronze is a part (this is the matter in which the form is) and the angle is a part. Again, the things in the account that shows each thing are parts of the whole too: so the genus is called a part of the species as well, though in another way the species is part of the genus.
paragraphs.greek: μέρος λέγεται ἕνα μὲν τρόπον εἰς ὃ διαιρεθείη ἂν τὸ ποσὸν ὁπωσοῦν (ἀεὶ γὰρ τὸ ἀφαιρούμενον τοῦ ποσοῦ ᾗ ποσὸν μέρος λέγεται ἐκείνου, οἷον τῶν τριῶν τὰ δύο μέρος λέγεταί πως), ἄλλον δὲ τρόπον τὰ καταμετροῦντα τῶν τοιούτων μόνον· διὸ τὰ δύο τῶν τριῶν ἔστι μὲν ὡς λέγεται μέρος, ἔστι δʼ ὡς οὔ. ἔτι εἰς ἃ τὸ εἶδος διαιρεθείη ἂν ἄνευ τοῦ ποσοῦ, καὶ ταῦτα μόρια λέγεται τούτου· διὸ τὰ εἴδη τοῦ γένους φασὶν εἶναι μόρια. ἔτι εἰς ἃ διαιρεῖται ἢ ἐξ ὧν σύγκειται τὸ ὅλον, ἢ τὸ εἶδος ἢ τὸ ἔχον τὸ εἶδος, οἷον τῆς σφαίρας τῆς χαλκῆς ἢ τοῦ κύβου τοῦ χαλκοῦ καὶ ὁ χαλκὸς μέρος (τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶν ἡ ὕλη ἐν ᾗ τὸ εἶδος) καὶ ἡ γωνία μέρος. ἔτι τὰ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ δηλοῦντι ἕκαστον, καὶ ταῦτα μόρια τοῦ ὅλου· διὸ τὸ γένος τοῦ εἴδους καὶ μέρος λέγεται, ἄλλως δὲ τὸ εἶδος τοῦ γένους μέρος.

flags.taylor: and the characteristic angle are parts
flags.why: Ross's "characteristic" is his own addition: the Greek says only "the angle" (ἡ γωνία), which is part of the form of the cube, as the bronze is part of its matter.

notes: Plato's Parmenides (137c-d, 142d-145a) and Theaetetus (204a-205e) ask how a whole is related to its parts, and whether the whole is something besides them; Aristotle's next chapter gives his answer for the word.

paragraphs.modern: "Whole" is said of that from which no part is absent of those of which it is called by nature a whole; and of what so contains the things it contains that they are one. This is in two ways: either as each is one, or as the one is made of them. The universal, and what is said generally as being a whole, is universal as containing many things, by being said of each and by all of them being one as each is, as man, horse and god are, because all are living beings. And the continuous and limited is a whole, when it is one thing made of many that are present in it, above all in potency, or if not, in actuality. Of these themselves, things that are such by nature are wholes more than those by art, as we said of the one too, wholeness being a kind of oneness.
paragraphs.greek: ὅλον λέγεται οὗ τε μηθὲν ἄπεστι μέρος ἐξ ὧν λέγεται ὅλον φύσει, καὶ τὸ περιέχον τὰ περιεχόμενα ὥστε ἕν τι εἶναι ἐκεῖνα· τοῦτο δὲ διχῶς· ἢ γὰρ ὡς ἕκαστον ἓν ἢ ὡς ἐκ τούτων τὸ ἕν. τὸ μὲν γὰρ καθόλου, καὶ τὸ ὅλως λεγόμενον ὡς ὅλον τι ὄν, οὕτως ἐστὶ καθόλου ὡς πολλὰ περιέχον τῷ κατηγορεῖσθαι καθʼ ἑκάστου καὶ ἓν ἅπαντα εἶναι ὡς ἕκαστον, οἷον ἄνθρωπον ἵππον θεόν, διότι ἅπαντα ζῷα· τὸ δὲ συνεχὲς καὶ πεπερασμένον, ὅταν ἕν τι ἐκ πλειόνων ᾖ, ἐνυπαρχόντων μάλιστα μὲν δυνάμει, εἰ δὲ μή, ἐνεργείᾳ. τούτων δʼ αὐτῶν μᾶλλον τὰ φύσει ἢ τέχνῃ τοιαῦτα, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑνὸς ἐλέγομεν, ὡς οὔσης τῆς ὁλότητος ἑνότητός τινος.

flags.taylor: e.g. man, horse, god, are one, because all are living things
flags.why: Ross's words are right; the Greek ζῷα is "animals", "living beings", and Aristotle counts god among them: god, Book Λ says (1072b28-30), is a living being, eternal and most good. For the Platonists the example is less strange: the world itself is a living being, with soul and intellect (Timaeus 30b).

paragraphs.modern: Again, of a quantity that has a beginning, a middle and an end, those in which the position makes no difference are called a total, and those in which it does, a whole. Those that admit of both are both wholes and totals: these are the things whose nature stays the same when they are rearranged, but whose shape does not, as wax or a cloak; they are called both whole and total, for they have both. Water, all liquids and number are called totals, but "the whole number" or "the whole water" is not said, except by a transfer of the word. Things are called "all", in the plural, of which "total" is said as of one, when they are taken as divided: "this total number", "all these units".
paragraphs.greek: ἔτι τοῦ ποσοῦ ἔχοντος δὲ ἀρχὴν καὶ μέσον καὶ ἔσχατον, ὅσων μὲν μὴ ποιεῖ ἡ θέσις διαφοράν, πᾶν λέγεται, ὅσων δὲ ποιεῖ, ὅλον. ὅσα δὲ ἄμφω ἐνδέχεται, καὶ ὅλα καὶ πάντα· ἔστι δὲ ταῦτα ὅσων ἡ μὲν φύσις ἡ αὐτὴ μένει τῇ μεταθέσει, ἡ δὲ μορφὴ οὔ, οἷον κηρὸς καὶ ἱμάτιον· καὶ γὰρ ὅλον καὶ πᾶν λέγεται· ἔχει γὰρ ἄμφω. ὕδωρ δὲ καὶ ὅσα ὑγρὰ καὶ ἀριθμὸς πᾶν μὲν λέγεται, ὅλος δʼ ἀριθμὸς καὶ ὅλον ὕδωρ οὐ λέγεται, ἂν μὴ μεταφορᾷ. πάντα δὲ λέγεται ἐφʼ οἷς τὸ πᾶν ὡς ἐφʼ ἑνί, ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ πάντα ὡς ἐπὶ διῃρημένοις· πᾶς οὗτος ὁ ἀριθμός, πᾶσαι αὗται αἱ μονάδες.

flags.taylor: those to which the position does not make a difference are called totals
flags.why: Ross's "totals" render πᾶν, the Greek for "all", "every", said of what is one: "all the water", "the whole number". English cannot keep πᾶν and its plural πάντα apart in the same word, and the modern version says "total" and "all", as Ross does.

paragraphs.modern: "Mutilated" is said not of any quantity whatever: it must be divisible and a whole. Two is not mutilated if one of its ones is taken away (for the part taken off by mutilation is never equal to what is left), nor is any number at all; for the substance must remain: if a cup is mutilated, it must still be a cup, but the number is no longer the same. Besides, not even all things with unlike parts can be mutilated (for a number has in a way unlike parts, as two and three); but in general nothing whose position makes no difference is mutilated, as water or fire: things must be such as to have position in their substance. Again, they must be continuous: for a scale is made of unlike notes and has position, but does not become mutilated. Besides, not even things that are wholes are mutilated by the privation of any part whatever. The parts must be neither the chief parts of the substance nor parts anywhere at all: a cup is not mutilated if it is bored through, but only if the handle or some extremity is taken; and a man is not mutilated if he loses flesh or the spleen, but only some extremity, and not every one, but one which, once taken off altogether, does not grow again. That is why the bald are not mutilated.
paragraphs.greek: κολοβὸν δὲ λέγεται τῶν ποσῶν οὐ τὸ τυχόν, ἀλλὰ μεριστόν τε δεῖ αὐτὸ εἶναι καὶ ὅλον. τά τε γὰρ δύο οὐ κολοβὰ θατέρου ἀφαιρουμένου ἑνός (οὐ γὰρ ἴσον τὸ καλόβωμα καὶ τὸ λοιπὸν οὐδέποτʼ ἐστίν) οὐδʼ ὅλως ἀριθμὸς οὐδείς· καὶ γὰρ τὴν οὐσίαν δεῖ μένειν· εἰ κύλιξ κολοβός, ἔτι εἶναι κύλικα· ὁ δὲ ἀριθμὸς οὐκέτι ὁ αὐτός. πρὸς δὲ τούτοις κἂν ἀνομοιομερῆ ᾖ, οὐδὲ ταῦτα πάντα (ὁ γὰρ ἀριθμὸς ἔστιν ὡς καὶ ἀνόμοια ἔχει μέρη, οἷον δυάδα τριάδα), ἀλλʼ ὅλως ὧν μὴ ποιεῖ ἡ θέσις διαφορὰν οὐδὲν κολοβόν, οἷον ὕδωρ ἢ πῦρ, ἀλλὰ δεῖ τοιαῦτα εἶναι ἃ κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν θέσιν ἔχει. ἔτι συνεχῆ· ἡ γὰρ ἁρμονία ἐξ ἀνομοίων μὲν καὶ θέσιν ἔχει, κολοβὸς δὲ οὐ γίγνεται. πρὸς δὲ τούτοις οὐδʼ ὅσα ὅλα, οὐδὲ ταῦτα ὁτουοῦν μορίου στερήσει κολοβά. οὐ γὰρ δεῖ οὔτε τὰ κύρια τῆς οὐσίας οὔτε τὰ ὁπουοῦν ὄντα· οἷον ἂν τρυπηθῇ ἡ κύλιξ, οὐ κολοβός, ἀλλʼ ἂν τὸ οὖς ἢ ἀκρωτήριόν τι, καὶ ὁ ἄνθρωπος οὐκ ἐὰν σάρκα ἢ τὸν σπλῆνα, ἀλλʼ ἐὰν ἀκρωτήριόν τι, καὶ τοῦτο οὐ πᾶν ἀλλʼ ὃ μὴ ἔχει γένεσιν ἀφαιρεθὲν ὅλον. διὰ τοῦτο οἱ φαλακροὶ οὐ κολοβοί.

flags.taylor: for a musical scale consists of unlike parts
flags.why: Ross's "musical scale" renders ἁρμονία, the "attunement" or tuning of the strings, the order of unlike notes set in their places; the modern version says "scale". In Book Α he renders it so too (985b31).

flags.taylor: e. g.a cup is not mutilated if it is bored
flags.why: Ross's page has lost the end of the chapter (at 1024a), on the handle of the cup, the extremities of a man and the bald; the modern version follows the Greek.

paragraphs.modern: "Genus" or "race" is said, in one way, if there is a continuous generation of things that have the same form: we say "as long as the race of men exists", meaning as long as their generation is continuous. In another way, of that from which things come as from the first that moved them into being: so some are called Hellenes by race and others Ionians, because the one come from Hellen and the others from Ion as their first begetter; and more from the begetter than from the matter (though people get a race-name from the female too, as the descendants of Pyrrha). Again, as the plane is the genus of plane figures and the solid of solids: each of the figures is either a plane of such a kind or a solid of such a kind, and this is what underlies the differences. Again, in accounts, the first part present, which is said in the what-it-is, is the genus, and the qualities are called its differences. "Genus", then, is said in all these ways: by continuous generation of the same form; by the first mover of the same form; and as matter, for that of which the difference and the quality are is the underlying thing, which we call matter.
paragraphs.greek: γένος λέγεται τὸ μὲν ἐὰν ᾖ ἡ γένεσις συνεχὴς τῶν τὸ εἶδος ἐχόντων τὸ αὐτό, οἷον λέγεται ἕως ἂν ἀνθρώπων γένος ᾖ, ὅτι ἕως ἂν ᾖ ἡ γένεσις συνεχὴς αὐτῶν· τὸ δὲ ἀφʼ οὗ ἂν ὦσι πρώτου κινήσαντος εἰς τὸ εἶναι· οὕτω γὰρ λέγονται Ἕλληνες τὸ γένος οἱ δὲ Ἴωνες, τῷ οἱ μὲν ἀπὸ Ἕλληνος οἱ δὲ ἀπὸ Ἴωνος εἶναι πρώτου γεννήσαντος· καὶ μᾶλλον οἱ ἀπὸ τοῦ γεννήσαντος ἢ τῆς ὕλης (λέγονται γὰρ καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ θήλεος τὸ γένος, οἷον οἱ ἀπὸ Πύρρας). ἔτι δὲ ὡς τὸ ἐπίπεδον τῶν σχημάτων γένος τῶν ἐπιπέδων καὶ τὸ στερεὸν τῶν στερεῶν· ἕκαστον γὰρ τῶν σχημάτων τὸ μὲν ἐπίπεδον τοιονδὶ τὸ δὲ στερεόν ἐστι τοιονδί· τοῦτο δʼ ἐστὶ τὸ ὑποκείμενον ταῖς διαφοραῖς. ἔτι ὡς ἐν τοῖς λόγοις τὸ πρῶτον ἐνυπάρχον, ὃ λέγεται ἐν τῷ τί ἐστι, τοῦτο γένος, οὗ διαφοραὶ λέγονται αἱ ποιότητες. τὸ μὲν οὖν γένος τοσαυταχῶς λέγεται, τὸ μὲν κατὰ γένεσιν συνεχῆ τοῦ αὐτοῦ εἴδους, τὸ δὲ κατὰ τὸ πρῶτον κινῆσαν ὁμοειδές, τὸ δʼ ὡς ὕλη· οὗ γὰρ ἡ διαφορὰ καὶ ἡ ποιότης ἐστί, τοῦτʼ ἔστι τὸ ὑποκείμενον, ὃ λέγομεν ὕλην.

flags.taylor: in reference to the first mover which is of the same
flags.why: Ross's page has lost the end of this sentence (at 1024b), on genus as matter; the modern version follows the Greek. "Of the same form": the begetter is of the same kind as the begotten, a man from a man.

notes: Hellen, son of Deucalion and Pyrrha, was the father of the Greeks in legend; Ion, his grandson, of the Ionians. Pyrrha and Deucalion alone survived the great flood, and peopled the earth again by throwing stones over their shoulders. The Greek γένος is both "race" and "genus", the logician's word.

paragraphs.modern: Things are called other in genus whose first underlying thing is other, and of which neither is reduced to the other nor both to the same thing: so form and matter are other in genus; and so are whatever are said according to another figure of predication of being (for some of the things that are signify what a thing is, others a quality, and others as has been divided before). For these too are not reduced either to one another or to some one thing.
paragraphs.greek: ἕτερα δὲ τῷ γένει λέγεται ὧν ἕτερον τὸ πρῶτον ὑποκείμενον καὶ μὴ ἀναλύεται θάτερον εἰς θάτερον μηδʼ ἄμφω εἰς ταὐτόν, οἷον τὸ εἶδος καὶ ἡ ὕλη ἕτερον τῷ γένει, καὶ ὅσα καθʼ ἕτερον σχῆμα κατηγορίας τοῦ ὄντος λέγεται (τὰ μὲν γὰρ τί ἐστι σημαίνει τῶν ὄντων τὰ δὲ ποιόν τι τὰ δʼ ὡς διῄρηται πρότερον)· οὐδὲ γὰρ ταῦτα ἀναλύεται οὔτʼ εἰς ἄλληλα οὔτʼ εἰς ἕν τι.
notes: "As has been divided before": the list of the categories in chapter 7. That the categories cannot be reduced to one genus is why being is not a genus (Book Β, 998b22-27): its unity is "with reference to one thing", substance (Book Γ, chapter 2).

paragraphs.modern: "False" is said, in one way, of a thing as false: this either because it is not put together or cannot be put together, as is said of the diagonal being commensurate, or of your being seated; for of these one is false always, the other at times, and in this way they are not things that are. Or of things that are, but are by nature such as to appear either not such as they are or as things that are not, as shadow-painting and dreams: these are something, but not the things of which they produce the appearance. Things, then, are called false in this way, either because they themselves are not, or because the appearance that comes from them is of something that is not.
paragraphs.greek: τὸ ψεῦδος λέγεται ἄλλον μὲν τρόπον ὡς πρᾶγμα ψεῦδος, καὶ τούτου τὸ μὲν τῷ μὴ συγκεῖσθαι ἢ ἀδύνατον εἶναι συντεθῆναι (ὥσπερ λέγεται τὸ τὴν διάμετρον εἶναι σύμμετρον ἢ τὸ σὲ καθῆσθαι· τούτων γὰρ ψεῦδος τὸ μὲν ἀεὶ τὸ δὲ ποτέ· οὕτω γὰρ οὐκ ὄντα ταῦτἀ, τὰ δὲ ὅσα ἔστι μὲν ὄντα, πέφυκε μέντοι φαίνεσθαι ἢ μὴ οἷα) ἐστιν ἢ ἃ μὴ ἔστιν (οἷον ἡ σκιαγραφία καὶ τὰ ἐνύπνια· ταῦτα γὰρ ἔστι μέν τι, ἀλλʼ οὐχ ὧν ἐμποιεῖ τὴν φαντασίαν)·—πράγματα μὲν οὖν ψευδῆ οὕτω λέγεται, ἢ τῷ μὴ εἶναι αὐτὰ ἢ τῷ τὴν ἀπʼ αὐτῶν φαντασίαν μὴ ὄντος εἶναι·

flags.taylor: e.g. a sketch or a dream
flags.why: Ross's "sketch" renders σκιαγραφία, "shadow-painting", painting with light and shade that looks like the thing from far off, but not close by. Plato uses the word for the images of the senses and of opinion (Republic 365c, 523b, 583b; Theaetetus 208e; Phaedo 69b).

paragraphs.modern: A false account is the account of things that are not, in so far as it is false. So every account is false of anything other than that of which it is true: the account of the circle is false of the triangle. Of each thing there is in a way one account, that of what it is to be, and in a way many, since the thing itself and the thing with an affection are in a way the same, as Socrates and musical Socrates. (A false account is not an account of anything, simply.) That is why Antisthenes foolishly thought that nothing could be said except by its own account, one of one; from which it followed that there could be no contradiction, and almost no saying anything false. But it is possible to say each thing not only by its own account but by another's, altogether falsely, but also in a way truly: as eight is double by the account of two.
paragraphs.greek: λόγος δὲ ψευδὴς ὁ τῶν μὴ ὄντων, ᾗ ψευδής, διὸ πᾶς λόγος ψευδὴς ἑτέρου ἢ οὗ ἐστὶν ἀληθής, οἷον ὁ τοῦ κύκλου ψευδὴς τριγώνου. ἑκάστου δὲ λόγος ἔστι μὲν ὡς εἷς, ὁ τοῦ τί ἦν εἶναι, ἔστι δʼ ὡς πολλοί, ἐπεὶ ταὐτό πως αὐτὸ καὶ αὐτὸ πεπονθός, οἷον Σωκράτης καὶ Σωκράτης μουσικός (ὁ δὲ ψευδὴς λόγος οὐθενός ἐστιν ἁπλῶς λόγος)· διὸ Ἀντισθένης ᾤετο εὐήθως μηθὲν ἀξιῶν λέγεσθαι πλὴν τῷ οἰκείῳ λόγῳ, ἓν ἐφʼ ἑνός· ἐξ ὧν συνέβαινε μὴ εἶναι ἀντιλέγειν, σχεδὸν δὲ μηδὲ ψεύδεσθαι. ἔστι δʼ ἕκαστον λέγειν οὐ μόνον τῷ αὐτοῦ λόγῳ ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ ἑτέρου, ψευδῶς μὲν καὶ παντελῶς, ἔστι δʼ ὡς καὶ ἀληθῶς, ὥσπερ τὰ ὀκτὼ διπλάσια τῷ τῆς δυάδος λόγῳ.

flags.taylor: A false conception is the conception of non-existent objects
flags.why: Ross's "conception" renders λόγος, "account", "statement", what is said of a thing; the modern version says "account", as everywhere in this work. Antisthenes' claim is about speech: one name, one account, for one thing.

notes: Antisthenes, a follower of Socrates, held that a thing can be named but not defined, and that one cannot contradict, since two who speak of the same thing say the same, and two who say different things speak of different things. Plato's Euthydemus (285e-286c), Theaetetus (201e-202c) and Sophist (251b-c) answer views of this kind.

paragraphs.modern: Things, then, are called false in these ways; and a false man is one who readily and by choice deals in such accounts, not for anything else but for their own sake, and one who produces such accounts in others, as we say things are false that produce a false appearance. That is why the argument in the Hippias is misleading, that the same man is false and true. For it takes the false man to be the one who can deceive (and this is the one who knows and is wise); and further, that the man who is bad willingly is better. It takes this falsehood through induction: for the man who limps willingly is better than the one who limps unwillingly, taking "limping" to mean mimicking a limp; since if he were lame willingly, he would perhaps be worse, as with character, and so in this case.
paragraphs.greek: τὰ μὲν οὖν οὕτω λέγεται ψευδῆ, ἄνθρωπος δὲ ψευδὴς ὁ εὐχερὴς καὶ προαιρετικὸς τῶν τοιούτων λόγων, μὴ διʼ ἕτερόν τι ἀλλὰ διʼ αὐτό, καὶ ὁ ἄλλοις ἐμποιητικὸς τῶν τοιούτων λόγων, ὥσπερ καὶ τὰ πράγματά φαμεν ψευδῆ εἶναι ὅσα ἐμποιεῖ φαντασίαν ψευδῆ. διὸ ὁ ἐν τῷ Ἱππίᾳ λόγος παρακρούεται ὡς ὁ αὐτὸς ψευδὴς καὶ ἀληθής. τὸν δυνάμενον γὰρ ψεύσασθαι λαμβάνει ψευδῆ (οὗτος δʼ ὁ εἰδὼς καὶ ὁ φρόνιμος)· ἔτι τὸν ἑκόντα φαῦλον βελτίω. τοῦτο δὲ ψεῦδος λαμβάνει διὰ τῆς ἐπαγωγῆς—ὁ γὰρ ἑκὼν χωλαίνων τοῦ ἄκοντος κρείττων—τὸ χωλαίνειν τὸ μιμεῖσθαι λέγων, ἐπεὶ εἴ γε χωλὸς ἑκών, χείρων ἴσως, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τοῦ ἤθους, καὶ οὗτος.

flags.taylor: This is a false result of zduction
flags.why: Ross's words are right, the OCR aside: "induction" (ἐπαγωγή) is the leading on from examples, the runner, the wrestler, the archer, by which Socrates in the Hippias Minor (373c-376b) reaches the conclusion that he who errs willingly is better than he who errs unwillingly. The Platonists read that conclusion as Plato's irony: no one who knows the good does wrong willingly.

notes: "Wise" here is φρόνιμος, "sensible", "of practical wisdom". The Hippias Minor (365b-369b) argues that the false man and the true are the same, since the one who knows can lie best.

paragraphs.modern: "Accident" is said of what belongs to something and can be truly said of it, but neither of necessity nor for the most part: as if someone, digging a hole for a plant, found treasure. The finding of treasure is an accident to the one digging the hole: for the one does not come of necessity from the other or after it, nor, for the most part, if one plants, does one find treasure. And a musical man might be pale; but since this does not come about of necessity or for the most part, we call it an accident. So, since there are things that belong, and belong to things, and some of them belong somewhere and at some time, whatever belongs, but not because it was this, or now, or here, will be an accident. Nor is there any definite cause of the accident, but only chance, and this is indefinite. Going to Aegina was an accident to someone, if he did not arrive there in order to go there, but because he was driven off course by a storm or captured by pirates. The accident has come about, or is, but not as itself, but as something else: for the storm was the cause of his coming to a place he was not sailing for, and this was Aegina.
paragraphs.greek: συμβεβηκὸς λέγεται ὃ ὑπάρχει μέν τινι καὶ ἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν, οὐ μέντοι οὔτʼ ἐξ ἀνάγκης οὔτε ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ, οἷον εἴ τις ὀρύττων φυτῷ βόθρον εὗρε θησαυρόν. τοῦτο τοίνυν συμβεβηκὸς τῷ ὀρύττοντι τὸν βόθρον, τὸ εὑρεῖν θησαυρόν· οὔτε γὰρ ἐξ ἀνάγκης τοῦτο ἐκ τούτου ἢ μετὰ τοῦτο, οὔθʼ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ ἄν τις φυτεύῃ θησαυρὸν εὑρίσκει. καὶ μουσικός γʼ ἄν τις εἴη λευκός· ἀλλʼ ἐπεὶ οὔτε ἐξ ἀνάγκης οὔθʼ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ τοῦτο γίγνεται, συμβεβηκὸς αὐτὸ λέγομεν. ὥστʼ ἐπεὶ ἔστιν ὑπάρχον τι καὶ τινί, καὶ ἔνια τούτων καὶ ποὺ καὶ ποτέ, ὅ τι ἂν ὑπάρχῃ μέν, ἀλλὰ μὴ διότι τοδὶ ἦν ἢ νῦν ἢ ἐνταῦθα, συμβεβηκὸς ἔσται. οὐδὲ δὴ αἴτιον ὡρισμένον οὐδὲν τοῦ συμβεβηκότος ἀλλὰ τὸ τυχόν· τοῦτο δʼ ἀόριστον. συνέβη τῳ εἰς Αἴγιναν ἐλθεῖν, εἰ μὴ διὰ τοῦτο ἀφίκετο ὅπως ἐκεῖ ἔλθῃ, ἀλλʼ ὑπὸ χειμῶνος ἐξωσθεὶς ἢ ὑπὸ λῃστῶν ληφθείς. γέγονε μὲν δὴ ἢ ἔστι τὸ συμβεβηκός, ἀλλʼ οὐχ ᾗ αὐτὸ ἀλλʼ ᾗ ἕτερον· ὁ γὰρ χειμὼν αἴτιος τοῦ μὴ ὅπου ἔπλει ἐλθεῖν, τοῦτο δʼ ἦν Αἴγινα.

flags.taylor: Accident is called that which is inherent in something
flags.why: Taylor's "inherent" renders ὑπάρχει, "belongs to"; the modern version says "belongs". The Greek συμβεβηκός, from συμβαίνειν, "to go along with", "to happen", is what happens to go with a thing, not what is in it by its nature.

notes: Book Ε (chapters 2 and 3) returns to the accident: there can be no science of it, since every science is of what is always or for the most part; and Physics II (chapters 4 to 6) on chance and luck.

paragraphs.modern: "Accident" is said in another way too: of whatever belongs to each thing in itself without being in its substance, as having its angles equal to two right angles belongs to the triangle. These can be eternal, but none of the others can. The account of this is given elsewhere.
paragraphs.greek: λέγεται δὲ καὶ ἄλλως συμβεβηκός, οἷον ὅσα ὑπάρχει ἑκάστῳ καθʼ αὑτὸ μὴ ἐν τῇ οὐσίᾳ ὄντα, οἷον τῷ τριγώνῳ τὸ δύο ὀρθὰς ἔχειν. καὶ ταῦτα μὲν ἐνδέχεται ἀΐδια εἶναι, ἐκείνων δὲ οὐδέν. λόγος δὲ τούτου ἐν ἑτέροις.

flags.taylor: This is explained elsewhere
flags.why: Ross's words are right; "elsewhere" is the Posterior Analytics (I.6, 75a18-22, and I.7), where such attributes, the "accidents in themselves" (καθ' αὑτὰ συμβεβηκότα), are what a science demonstrates of its subject. The later schools called them "properties".

paragraphs.modern: We are looking for the principles and causes of the things that are, and clearly of them as things that are. There is a cause of health and of good condition, and the objects of mathematics have principles, elements and causes; and in general every science that uses thought, or has any share in thought, deals with causes and principles, more exact or more simple. But all these sciences mark off some one being, some one kind, and busy themselves with that, not with being simply, nor as being; and they give no account of what that thing is. They start from it, some making it plain to the senses, others taking what it is as a hypothesis, and so they demonstrate, more strictly or more loosely, the attributes that belong in themselves to the kind they are about. So it is clear that from such a survey there is no demonstration of substance, or of what a thing is, but some other way of making it known. Likewise they say nothing of whether the kind they deal with is or is not; for it belongs to the same thinking to make plain what a thing is and that it is.
paragraphs.greek: αἱ ἀρχαὶ καὶ τὰ αἴτια ζητεῖται τῶν ὄντων, δῆλον δὲ ὅτι ᾗ ὄντα. ἔστι γάρ τι αἴτιον ὑγιείας καὶ εὐεξίας, καὶ τῶν μαθηματικῶν εἰσὶν ἀρχαὶ καὶ στοιχεῖα καὶ αἴτια, καὶ ὅλως δὲ πᾶσα ἐπιστήμη διανοητικὴ ἢ μετέχουσά τι διανοίας περὶ αἰτίας καὶ ἀρχάς ἐστιν ἢ ἀκριβεστέρας ἢ ἁπλουστέρας. ἀλλὰ πᾶσαι αὗται περὶ ὄν τι καὶ γένος τι περιγραψάμεναι περὶ τούτου πραγματεύονται, ἀλλʼ οὐχὶ περὶ ὄντος ἁπλῶς οὐδὲ ᾗ ὄν, οὐδὲ τοῦ τί ἐστιν οὐθένα λόγον ποιοῦνται, ἀλλʼ ἐκ τούτου, αἱ μὲν αἰσθήσει ποιήσασαι αὐτὸ δῆλον αἱ δʼ ὑπόθεσιν λαβοῦσαι τὸ τί ἐστιν, οὕτω τὰ καθʼ αὑτὰ ὑπάρχοντα τῷ γένει περὶ ὅ εἰσιν ἀποδεικνύουσιν ἢ ἀναγκαιότερον ἢ μαλακώτερον· διόπερ φανερὸν ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἀπόδειξις οὐσίας οὐδὲ τοῦ τί ἐστιν ἐκ τῆς τοιαύτης ἐπαγωγῆς, ἀλλά τις ἄλλος τρόπος τῆς δηλώσεως. ὁμοίως δὲ οὐδʼ εἰ ἔστιν ἢ μὴ ἔστι τὸ γένος περὶ ὃ πραγματεύονται οὐδὲν λέγουσι, διὰ τὸ τῆς αὐτῆς εἶναι διανοίας τό τε τί ἐστι δῆλον ποιεῖν καὶ εἰ ἔστιν.—

flags.taylor: every dianoetic science, or which participates any thing of the dianoetic power
flags.why: Taylor's "dianoetic" is the Greek διανοητική carried over: the science that works by thought, by reasoning step by step (διάνοια), as against the senses. In the Platonists' scheme of the Republic (511d-e) διάνοια is the reasoning of the mathematician, below intellect (νοῦς); Aristotle uses the word more widely, of any science that reasons. The modern version says "uses thought".

notes: "No demonstration of substance": a definition is not proved but grasped or shown; the Posterior Analytics (II.3-10) argues it at length. The sciences take what their subject is, and that it is, as given; the science of being as being examines both.

paragraphs.modern: Now natural science too happens to be about one kind of being: it is about the kind of substance that has the principle of its motion and rest in itself. So clearly it is neither practical nor productive. In things made, the principle is in the maker, either intellect, or art, or some power; in things done, it is in the doer, the choice: for what is done and what is chosen are the same. So if every thought is either practical, or productive, or theoretical, natural science must be some theoretical science; but theoretical about the kind of being that can be moved, and about substance that, by its account, is for the most part not separable on its own.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ ἡ φυσικὴ ἐπιστήμη τυγχάνει οὖσα περὶ γένος τι τοῦ ὄντος (περὶ γὰρ τὴν τοιαύτην ἐστὶν οὐσίαν ἐν ᾗ ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως καὶ στάσεως ἐν αὐτᾖ, δῆλον ὅτι οὔτε πρακτική ἐστιν οὔτε ποιητική (τῶν μὲν γὰρ ποιητῶν ἐν τῷ ποιοῦντι ἡ ἀρχή, ἢ νοῦς ἢ τέχνη ἢ δύναμίς τις, τῶν δὲ πρακτῶν ἐν τῷ πράττοντι, ἡ προαίρεσις· τὸ αὐτὸ γὰρ τὸ πρακτὸν καὶ προαιρετόν), ὥστε εἰ πᾶσα διάνοια ἢ πρακτικὴ ἢ ποιητικὴ ἢ θεωρητική, ἡ φυσικὴ θεωρητική τις ἂν εἴη, ἀλλὰ θεωρητικὴ περὶ τοιοῦτον ὂν ὅ ἐστι δυνατὸν κινεῖσθαι, καὶ περὶ οὐσίαν τὴν κατὰ τὸν λόγον ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ ὡς οὐ χωριστὴν μόνον.

flags.taylor: viz. will, for that which is done and that
flags.why: Ross's "will" renders προαίρεσις, "choice", the deliberate choice that Aristotle sets at the head of action (Nicomachean Ethics III.2-3); Taylor says "free-will". Both read a later idea of the will into the word; the modern version says "choice", as in Book Δ (V.1).

flags.taylor: only about that kind of substance which in respect of its definition is for the most part not separable from matter
flags.why: The Greek is compressed: "about substance that is according to its account, for the most part, as not separable only". Ross supplies "from matter", which the sense needs: the natural scientist defines things, for the most part, together with their matter, as the next lines show with "snub". Taylor reads the words otherwise ("known through definition, and has not alone a separate subsistence").

paragraphs.modern: We must not fail to notice how what it is to be, and the account, stand: without this, inquiry does nothing. Of things defined, and of the "what is it" of things, some are like the snub and some like the concave. These differ in that the snub is taken together with its matter (the snub is a concave nose), while concavity is without perceptible matter. If, then, all natural things are said in the way the snub is (nose, eye, face, flesh, bone, and animal in general; leaf, root, bark, and plant in general; for the account of none of them is without motion, but always has matter), it is clear how we must look for and define what a thing is in natural things, and why it belongs to the student of nature to study some of the soul too: as much of it as is not without matter. That natural science is theoretical, then, is plain from this.
paragraphs.greek: δεῖ δὲ τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι καὶ τὸν λόγον πῶς ἐστὶ μὴ λανθάνειν, ὡς ἄνευ γε τούτου τὸ ζητεῖν μηδέν ἐστι ποιεῖν. ἔστι δὲ τῶν ὁριζομένων καὶ τῶν τί ἐστι τὰ μὲν ὡς τὸ σιμὸν τὰ δʼ ὡς τὸ κοῖλον. διαφέρει δὲ ταῦτα ὅτι τὸ μὲν σιμὸν συνειλημμένον ἐστὶ μετὰ τῆς ὕλης (ἔστι γὰρ τὸ σιμὸν κοίλη ῥίς), ἡ δὲ κοιλότης ἄνευ ὕλης αἰσθητῆς. εἰ δὴ πάντα τὰ φυσικὰ ὁμοίως τῷ σιμῷ λέγονται, οἷον ῥὶς ὀφθαλμὸς πρόσωπον σὰρξ ὀστοῦν, ὅλως ζῷον, φύλλον ῥίζα φλοιός, ὅλως φυτόν (οὐθενὸς γὰρ ἄνευ κινήσεως ὁ λόγος αὐτῶν, ἀλλʼ ἀεὶ ἔχει ὕλην), δῆλον πῶς δεῖ ἐν τοῖς φυσικοῖς τὸ τί ἐστι ζητεῖν καὶ ὁρίζεσθαι, καὶ διότι καὶ περὶ ψυχῆς ἐνίας θεωρῆσαι τοῦ φυσικοῦ, ὅση μὴ ἄνευ τῆς ὕλης ἐστίν.

flags.taylor: understand in what manner the formal cause and definition
flags.why: Taylor's "formal cause" renders τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι, "what it is to be", which the modern version says throughout this work (Ross: "essence"). The name "formal cause" is the later schools'.

notes: The snub (σιμόν) is Aristotle's standing example of a thing whose definition must name its matter: snubness is concavity in a nose. Book Ζ (chapters 5 and 10 to 11) returns to it. On the Soul (I.1, 403a-b) draws the same line: the student of nature defines anger as a boiling of the blood about the heart, the dialectician as a desire to hurt back.

paragraphs.modern: But mathematics is theoretical too. Whether its objects are unmoved and separate is not clear at present; but it is clear that some parts of mathematics study their objects as unmoved and as separate. If there is something eternal, unmoved and separate, plainly knowing it belongs to a theoretical science: not, however, to natural science (for natural science is about certain things that move), nor to mathematics, but to a science prior to both. Natural science is about things that are separate but not unmoved; some parts of mathematics are about things unmoved but probably not separate, rather as in matter; the first science is about things both separate and unmoved. All causes must be eternal, but these above all: for they are the causes of the divine things that are manifest to us. So there will be three theoretical philosophies, mathematics, natural science and theology; for it is not unclear that if the divine is present anywhere, it is present in a nature of this kind, and the most honourable science must be about the most honourable kind. The theoretical sciences, then, are more to be chosen than the others, and this one more than the other theoretical sciences.
paragraphs.greek: ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἡ φυσικὴ θεωρητική ἐστι, φανερὸν ἐκ τούτων· ἀλλʼ ἔστι καὶ ἡ μαθηματικὴ θεωρητική· ἀλλʼ εἰ ἀκινήτων καὶ χωριστῶν ἐστί, νῦν ἄδηλον, ὅτι μέντοι ἔνια μαθήματα ᾗ ἀκίνητα καὶ ᾗ χωριστὰ θεωρεῖ, δῆλον. εἰ δέ τί ἐστιν ἀΐδιον καὶ ἀκίνητον καὶ χωριστόν, φανερὸν ὅτι θεωρητικῆς τὸ γνῶναι, οὐ μέντοι φυσικῆς γε (περὶ κινητῶν γάρ τινων ἡ φυσικἤ οὐδὲ μαθηματικῆς, ἀλλὰ προτέρας ἀμφοῖν. ἡ μὲν γὰρ φυσικὴ περὶ χωριστὰ μὲν ἀλλʼ οὐκ ἀκίνητα, τῆς δὲ μαθηματικῆς ἔνια περὶ ἀκίνητα μὲν οὐ χωριστὰ δὲ ἴσως ἀλλʼ ὡς ἐν ὕλῃ· ἡ δὲ πρώτη καὶ περὶ χωριστὰ καὶ ἀκίνητα. ἀνάγκη δὲ πάντα μὲν τὰ αἴτια ἀΐδια εἶναι, μάλιστα δὲ ταῦτα· ταῦτα γὰρ αἴτια τοῖς φανεροῖς τῶν θείων. ὥστε τρεῖς ἂν εἶεν φιλοσοφίαι θεωρητικαί, μαθηματική, φυσική, θεολογική (οὐ γὰρ ἄδηλον ὅτι εἴ που τὸ θεῖον ὑπάρχει, ἐν τῇ τοιαύτῃ φύσει ὑπάρχεἰ, καὶ τὴν τιμιωτάτην δεῖ περὶ τὸ τιμιώτατον γένος εἶναι. αἱ μὲν οὖν θεωρητικαὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἐπιστημῶν αἱρετώταται, αὕτη δὲ τῶν θεωρητικῶν.

flags.taylor: what we may call theology
flags.why: The Greek says simply "theology" (θεολογική), with no "what we may call". Ross's hedge is his own. Aristotle names the first philosophy theology here and again in Book Κ (XI.7); for the Platonists it was the name of the whole summit of the course, and Proclus called his own work on the gods the Elements of Theology and the Platonic Theology.

flags.taylor: causes of so much of the divine as appears to us
flags.why: Ross's footnote takes "the divine things that are manifest to us" to be the movements of the heavenly bodies, which the unmoved causes of Book Λ (XII.8) move; Taylor keeps the Greek's "the phaenomena of things divine". The Platonists read the line of the visible gods, the stars, whose causes are the intelligible gods.

notes: "Separate" (χωριστόν): able to be on its own, not in something else. Natural things are separate but move; mathematical objects are unmoved but are not on their own, only in thought apart from the bodies they are in; the objects of first philosophy are both. Whether there are such, Book Λ (XII.6-8) argues.

paragraphs.modern: One might raise the puzzle whether first philosophy is universal, or about some one kind and some one nature. Not even the mathematical sciences are all alike in this: geometry and astronomy are about a certain nature, while universal mathematics is common to all. If there is no other substance besides those formed by nature, natural science would be the first science. But if there is some unmoved substance, the science of it is prior, and is first philosophy, and universal in this way, because it is first. And it would belong to this science to study being as being, both what it is and what belongs to it as being.
paragraphs.greek: ἀπορήσειε γὰρ ἄν τις πότερόν ποθʼ ἡ πρώτη φιλοσοφία καθόλου ἐστὶν ἢ περί τι γένος καὶ φύσιν τινὰ μίαν (οὐ γὰρ ὁ αὐτὸς τρόπος οὐδʼ ἐν ταῖς μαθηματικαῖς, ἀλλʼ ἡ μὲν γεωμετρία καὶ ἀστρολογία περί τινα φύσιν εἰσίν, ἡ δὲ καθόλου πασῶν κοινἤ· εἰ μὲν οὖν μὴ ἔστι τις ἑτέρα οὐσία παρὰ τὰς φύσει συνεστηκυίας, ἡ φυσικὴ ἂν εἴη πρώτη ἐπιστήμη· εἰ δʼ ἔστι τις οὐσία ἀκίνητος, αὕτη προτέρα καὶ φιλοσοφία πρώτη, καὶ καθόλου οὕτως ὅτι πρώτη· καὶ περὶ τοῦ ὄντος ᾗ ὂν ταύτης ἂν εἴη θεωρῆσαι, καὶ τί ἐστι καὶ τὰ ὑπάρχοντα ᾗ ὄν.
notes: The answer joins the science of being as being of Book Γ with the theology of Book Λ: the science of the first substance is universal because it is first, since all other things are called beings by their relation to substance, and substances to the first. The Platonists made the same move, from the One that is first to the One that is the cause of all.

paragraphs.modern: Being, said simply, is said in many ways. One of them, we saw, was being by accident; another, being as true, with not being as the false. Besides these there are the figures of the categories, as the what, the of-what-kind, the how-much, the where, the when, and anything else that signifies in this way; and again, besides all these, being potentially and actually. Since, then, being is said in many ways, we must first say of being by accident that there is no study of it. A sign of this is that no science troubles itself about it, practical, productive or theoretical. The one who makes a house does not make all the things that happen to go with the house as it comes to be: they are endless. Nothing prevents the house once made from being pleasant to some, harmful to others, useful to others, and different, one might say, from everything there is; and the art of building produces none of these. In the same way the geometer does not study the attributes that belong to figures in this way, nor whether "triangle" and "triangle with angles equal to two right angles" are different.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλʼ ἐπεὶ τὸ ὂν τὸ ἁπλῶς λεγόμενον λέγεται πολλαχῶς, ὧν ἓν μὲν ἦν τὸ κατὰ συμβεβηκός, ἕτερον δὲ τὸ ὡς ἀληθές, καὶ τὸ μὴ ὂν ὡς τὸ ψεῦδος, παρὰ ταῦτα δʼ ἐστὶ τὰ σχήματα τῆς κατηγορίας (οἷον τὸ μὲν τί, τὸ δὲ ποιόν, τὸ δὲ ποσόν, τὸ δὲ πού, τὸ δὲ ποτέ, καὶ εἴ τι ἄλλο σημαίνει τὸν τρόπον τοῦτον), ἔτι παρὰ ταῦτα πάντα τὸ δυνάμει καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ·—ἐπεὶ δὴ πολλαχῶς λέγεται τὸ ὄν, πρῶτον περὶ τοῦ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς λεκτέον, ὅτι οὐδεμία ἐστὶ περὶ αὐτὸ θεωρία. σημεῖον δέ· οὐδεμιᾷ γὰρ ἐπιστήμῃ ἐπιμελὲς περὶ αὐτοῦ οὔτε πρακτικῇ οὔτε ποιητικῇ οὔτε θεωρητικῇ. οὔτε γὰρ ὁ ποιῶν οἰκίαν ποιεῖ ὅσα συμβαίνει ἅμα τῇ οἰκίᾳ γιγνομένῃ (ἄπειρα γάρ ἐστιν· τοῖς μὲν γὰρ ἡδεῖαν τοῖς δὲ βλαβερὰν τοῖς δʼ ὠφέλιμον οὐθὲν εἶναι κωλύει τὴν ποιηθεῖσαν, καὶ ἑτέραν ὡς εἰπεῖν πάντων τῶν ὄντων· ὧν οὐθενός ἐστιν ἡ οἰκοδομικὴ ποιητικἤ, τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τρόπον οὐδʼ ὁ γεωμέτρης θεωρεῖ τὰ οὕτω συμβεβηκότα τοῖς σχήμασιν, οὐδʼ εἰ ἕτερόν ἐστι τρίγωνον καὶ τρίγωνον δύο ὀρθὰς ἔχον.

flags.taylor: nor whether a wooden triangle
flags.why: Taylor's "wooden" is not in the Greek, which asks only whether "triangle" and "triangle having two right angles" are different: whether a thing and that thing with an attribute are the same, a sophist's question. His text, or his reading of it, had something else.

notes: "We saw": in Book Δ (V.7), on the ways being is said. The four ways named here are the plan of the books that follow: being by accident and as true are set aside in this book; being in the categories, above all substance, is Books Ζ and Η; potency and actuality Book Θ.

paragraphs.modern: And this happens with good reason: the accident is, as it were, a mere name. That is why Plato, in a way, was not wrong to set sophistry in the region of what is not. For the sophists' arguments are about the accident, one might say, more than about anything: whether the musical and the literate are different or the same, and the musical Coriscus and Coriscus; and whether everything that is, but not always, has come to be, so that if someone who was musical has become literate, he has also, being literate, become musical; and all the other arguments of this kind. For the accident appears to be something close to what is not. This is clear also from such arguments as these: of things that are in another way there is coming to be and passing away, but of things that are by accident there is not. Still, we must say further, as far as we can, what the nature of the accident is and from what cause it is; for at the same time it will perhaps be clear why there is no science of it.
paragraphs.greek: καὶ τοῦτʼ εὐλόγως συμπίπτει· ὥσπερ γὰρ ὄνομά τι μόνον τὸ συμβεβηκός ἐστιν. διὸ Πλάτων τρόπον τινὰ οὐ κακῶς τὴν σοφιστικὴν περὶ τὸ μὴ ὂν ἔταξεν. εἰσὶ γὰρ οἱ τῶν σοφιστῶν λόγοι περὶ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς ὡς εἰπεῖν μάλιστα πάντων, πότερον ἕτερον ἢ ταὐτὸν μουσικὸν καὶ γραμματικόν, καὶ μουσικὸς Κορίσκος καὶ Κορίσκος, καὶ εἰ πᾶν ὃ ἂν ᾖ, μὴ ἀεὶ δέ, γέγονεν, ὥστʼ εἰ μουσικὸς ὢν γραμματικὸς γέγονε, καὶ γραμματικὸς ὢν μουσικός, καὶ ὅσοι δὴ ἄλλοι τοιοῦτοι τῶν λόγων εἰσίν· φαίνεται γὰρ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς ἐγγύς τι τοῦ μὴ ὄντος. δῆλον δὲ καὶ ἐκ τῶν τοιούτων λόγων· τῶν μὲν γὰρ ἄλλον τρόπον ὄντων ἔστι γένεσις καὶ φθορά, τῶν δὲ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς οὐκ ἔστιν. ἀλλʼ ὅμως λεκτέον ἔτι περὶ τοῦ συμβεβηκότος ἐφʼ ὅσον ἐνδέχεται, τίς ἡ φύσις αὐτοῦ καὶ διὰ τίνʼ αἰτίαν ἔστιν· ἅμα γὰρ δῆλον ἴσως ἔσται καὶ διὰ τί ἐπιστήμη οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτοῦ.—

flags.taylor: whether ‘ musical ’ and ‘lettered’ are different
flags.why: Ross's "lettered" is γραμματικός, the one who knows his letters, who can read and write: "literate". The modern version says "literate".

notes: Plato's Sophist (254a) places the sophist "in the darkness of what is not", where he is hard to see; the Stranger's hunt for him ends with the account of not being as difference. Coriscus is Aristotle's stock example of a particular man, perhaps the Coriscus of Scepsis who was with him at Assos.

paragraphs.modern: Since among the things that are, some are always in the same state and of necessity (not necessity in the sense of force, but the necessity we mean when we say a thing cannot be otherwise), and others are not of necessity nor always, but for the most part, this is the principle and this the cause of there being an accident: for what is neither always nor for the most part, this we call an accident. If there is wintry, cold weather in the dog days, we say that this happened by accident, but not if there is stifling heat; for the one is always or for the most part, the other not. It is an accident that a man is pale (for this is neither always nor for the most part), but it is not by accident that he is an animal. It is an accident that the builder makes someone healthy, because it is not the builder's nature to do this but the doctor's: the builder happened to be a doctor. And a cook, aiming at pleasure, might make something healthy, but not by the art of cooking: so we say it happened by accident; and there is a way in which he makes it, but simply he does not. For of other things there are sometimes powers that produce them, but of these there is no art and no definite power; for of things that are or come to be by accident, the cause too is by accident.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπεὶ οὖν ἐστὶν ἐν τοῖς οὖσι τὰ μὲν ἀεὶ ὡσαύτως ἔχοντα καὶ ἐξ ἀνάγκης, οὐ τῆς κατὰ τὸ βίαιον λεγομένης ἀλλʼ ἣν λέγομεν τῷ μὴ ἐνδέχεσθαι ἄλλως, τὰ δʼ ἐξ ἀνάγκης μὲν οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδʼ ἀεί, ὡς δʼ ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ, αὕτη ἀρχὴ καὶ αὕτη αἰτία ἐστὶ τοῦ εἶναι τὸ συμβεβηκός· ὃ γὰρ ἂν ᾖ μήτʼ ἀεὶ μήθʼ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ, τοῦτό φαμεν συμβεβηκὸς εἶναι. οἷον ἐπὶ κυνὶ ἂν χειμὼν γένηται καὶ ψῦχος, τοῦτο συμβῆναί φαμεν, ἀλλʼ οὐκ ἂν πνῖγος καὶ ἀλέα, ὅτι τὸ μὲν ἀεὶ ἢ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ τὸ δʼ οὔ. καὶ τὸν ἄνθρωπον λευκὸν εἶναι συμβέβηκεν (οὔτε γὰρ ἀεὶ οὔθʼ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὔ, ζῷον δʼ οὐ κατὰ συμβεβηκός. καὶ τὸ ὑγιάζειν δὲ τὸν οἰκοδόμον συμβεβηκός, ὅτι οὐ πέφυκε τοῦτο ποιεῖν οἰκοδόμος ἀλλὰ ἰατρός, ἀλλὰ συνέβη ἰατρὸν εἶναι τὸν οἰκοδόμον. καὶ ὀψοποιὸς ἡδονῆς στοχαζόμενος ποιήσειεν ἄν τι ὑγιεινόν, ἀλλʼ οὐ κατὰ τὴν ὀψοποιητικήν· διὸ συνέβη, φαμέν, καὶ ἔστιν ὡς ποιεῖ, ἁπλῶς δʼ οὔ. τῶν μὲν γὰρ ἄλλων [ἐνίοτε] δυνάμεις εἰσὶν αἱ ποιητικαί, τῶν δʼ οὐδεμία τέχνη οὐδὲ δύναμις ὡρισμένη· τῶν γὰρ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ὄντων ἢ γιγνομένων καὶ τὸ αἴτιόν ἐστι κατὰ συμβεβηκός.

flags.taylor: a confectioner, aiming at giving pleasure
flags.why: Ross's "confectioner" is ὀψοποιός, the cook who prepares savoury dishes; Plato's Gorgias (464d-465b) sets the cook's knack, aimed at pleasure, against medicine, aimed at health. The modern version says "cook", as Taylor does.

flags.taylor: sometimes tend to be produced by alien potencies
flags.why: The Greek, which the 1924 text brackets in part ("sometimes"), says only that "of other things there are powers that produce them": of what is not by accident there is a definite power or art that makes it, of the accident none. Ross's "alien potencies" reads the line otherwise.

notes: "The dog days" (ἐπὶ κυνί): the hottest weeks of summer, when the Dog Star rises with the sun; Taylor has "when the sun is in Canis".

paragraphs.modern: So, since not everything is or comes to be of necessity and always, but most things for the most part, there must be being by accident. The pale man, for instance, is musical neither always nor for the most part; but since this sometimes happens, it will be by accident (otherwise everything will be of necessity). So the cause of the accident will be the matter, which can be otherwise than it is for the most part. We must take as our starting point this question: is there nothing that is neither always nor for the most part? Or is that impossible? There is, then, something besides these, which falls out either way, and by accident. But is there the for-the-most-part, and does the always belong to nothing, or are there some eternal things?
